title: Token Budget Enforcement as a Cheap Defense: Does Forcing Short Responses Reduce Jailbreak Utility?

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: token-limit enforcement is a trivially deployable API-level control. Either it degrades jailbreak utility (underexplored practical defense) or partial outputs remain harmful (debunking a common practitioner misconception). Both outcomes are immediately actionable.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Accessible: pure inference experiment. Set max_tokens parameter to 3 values, run existing prefilling attacks, score with existing StrongReject Likert evaluator. No custom code beyond standard API calls needed.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: one model, one attack type, 3 token limit conditions, existing evaluator. Results fit in a single comparison table. Easily completable well within 30 hours.

evidence: No published study was found that systematically evaluates max_tokens enforcement as a jailbreak defense mechanism.
Token limit research focuses on context window management and input truncation rather than output truncation as a safety measure.
The BOOST attack (2025) exploits eos tokens for jailbreaking, showing token-level manipulation is a live research area, but from the attack side rather than defense.
Talk Too Much (2024) studies poisoning under token limits but from an attack perspective, not evaluating truncation as defense.
The simple hypothesis that truncated harmful outputs may have reduced utility is intuitive but untested empirically.
